title: The death of a friend (4.4–4.9)
hook: his closest friend dies and everything becomes death to him
tomorrow: after a grave like that, is it safe to love again?

segments.voice: Last week ended with Monica's dream: where you are, he is too. The line was the same rule, and a mother who waited on it.

Some people keep a friend's number in their phone long after the funeral, and never quite delete the thread. Augustine would understand. Back in his hometown, a young teacher now, he had a friend he grew up with, who shared his studies and his ideas. That friendship, he says, was sweeter to him than anything else in his life then. Who was he? The Confessions never gives his name. Then the friend falls ill with a fever, and lies unconscious, and his family does something Augustine doesn't expect.
screen: `THE NUMBER NOBODY DELETES.` → `A FRIEND FROM CHILDHOOD.` → `A FEVER, AND A SURPRISE.`

segments.voice: They have him baptized. Augustine, who had led him away from the faith, assumes it means nothing, and when the friend wakes, he jokes about it. The friend turns on him, he says, as if he were an enemy, and tells him to stop if he wants to stay his friend. Augustine holds back, meaning to bring it up later. There is no later. A few days on, the fever returns, and his friend dies while Augustine is away. Then the grief. In Pusey's words: "At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death." His hometown became a torment. He looked for his friend everywhere, and every place only said he wasn't coming. He became a great question to himself, he says, and only weeping was sweet. Looking back, he borrows an old poet's phrase for a friend, "half of my soul," and says it felt like one soul in two bodies. Here's the part to tell someone tonight: the friend's last real conversation with Augustine was a rebuke, defending a baptism Augustine had laughed at. The older Augustine, writing to God, doesn't hide it. He also sees what had gone wrong in the loving, and that's where tomorrow picks up.
screen: `BAPTIZED WHILE UNCONSCIOUS.` · `A JOKE, AND A REBUKE.` · `WHATEVER I BEHELD WAS DEATH.` · `ONE SOUL IN TWO BODIES.` · then, large: `HALF OF MY SOUL.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and remember a friend who has died, or anyone dear you've lost, and let one ordinary detail come back: a laugh, a phrase, the way they said your name. Stay with it gently, without hurrying the grief along or pushing it away. If you pray, you can commend them to God by name; if not, just keep the detail company until the bell.
The death of a friend. Augustine's grief for the friend of his youth, when everything he looked at was death, and half his soul seemed gone.
screen: `THE DEATH OF A FRIEND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: half of my soul, the name grief gives to love that has nowhere to go. Be gentle tonight.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for those who have died, have Masses offered for them, and remember them together on All Souls' Day.

notes: For parents: this lesson is about the death of a young man and a grieving friend; told gently, with no detail of the illness beyond a fever. The chat touches an elder's grief (Abuela's friend).
Pusey 4.4.9: 'At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death.' Confirm exact wording. Latin for the original game: 'et quidquid aspiciebam mors erat'. Confirm.

Pusey 4.6.11 renders the friend as 'Thou half of my soul' (from Horace, Odes 1.3, 'animae dimidium meae'); only 'half of my soul' is quoted. Augustine does not name Horace; the voice says 'an old poet'. Confirm.

Paraphrased from 4.4: friend from childhood, shared studies; Augustine had turned him toward Manichaean error (voice: 'led him away from the faith'); baptized while unconscious; the rebuke; fever returned a few days later and he died in Augustine's absence; hometown a torment; 'I became a great riddle/question to myself'; only tears sweet. From 4.6: one soul in two bodies. Confirm.
The friend is unnamed in the Confessions; the myth item relies on this.
4.6 also mentions Augustine being weary of life and afraid to die; left out on purpose. A Keeper may wish to add crisis-care wording if any later day includes it.
